content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper proposed a method named IEG (the first letters of isolation, escalation and guidance) for robust neural network training with severe label noises. Specifically, the letters of IEG mean isolation of noisy labels, escalation of useful supervision from mislabeled data, and guidance from small trusted data. Therefore, the method is a combination of 3 components.

In fact, "I" is just the sample selection direction in learning with noisy labels, and "E" is just the label correction direction in learning with noisy labels. They are 2 out of 3 famous directions when there are only training data with noisy labels. The direction of "G" is also quite famous when there are also a small set of clean validation data. These directions are conceptually orthogonal, and this is known for long time in this area. A combination of them cannot make the novelty above the threshold of a very competitive ML conference like ICLR! Note that this is an academic/scientific paper, not an industrial product, so you don't need to combine all things that might work.

BTW, in "E", no useful *supervision* from mislabeled data is used; instead, some useful *information* from mislabeled data is used. The term supervision refers to the y part rather than the x part of the data in ML or at least in weakly-supervised learning.

display_title: Thanks for the comments. Detailed justifications of the rating will be really helpful.

content.title: Thanks for the comments. Detailed justifications of the rating will be really helpful.
content.comment:
Thanks for the review.  

First, please refer to the comment above for justification about the method contribution to resolve the potential misunderstanding here. Then we further address the specific questions/comments below.

1) The reviewer criticized the paper, by saying that I, E, and G are not three new "directions". 
 
    We do not agree with the conclusion about the line between "academic/scientific paper and industrial product" on our work.

    Looking back to noise label ML literature, many well-known concepts and directions are reused or re-visited over and over again in order to better understand and improve performance. The same as IEG, Isolation of noisy labels, escalation of useful supervision from mislabeled data, and guidance from small trusted data are three long-standing directions to solve noise label problems. **The contribution of the IEG is NOT opening new directions but a new METHOD with unprecedented performance on long-standing problems.

    More importantly, we are not the first one to consider them together as we argued in the comments to Reviewer 2. The huge performance difference is not because of blind combination, but careful re-designs and insights. They are the key to achieve success and they are comprehensively studied in ablation study.  


2) We believe that the reviewer misunderstood how IEG achieves Escalation "supervision" based on the last paragraph of the comments.

    E is actually supervision on the y part, NOT the x part. It is exactly what the proposed meta re-labeling and losses from $L_{\beta}^p$ and  $L_{\beta}^u$ does, which creates better y in order to trigger supervision. We encourage the reviewer to read the method part in detail and re-evaluate this judgment.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This paper combines several methods for dealing with label noise. Specifically, combining the idea of learning to reweight (Ren et al. 2018), pseudo labeling (Berthelot et al. 2019), MixUp regularization (Zhang et al. 2018 ICLR), etc. Excellent empirical results have been achieved. Sufficient details have been given to repeat the experiments. Overall, the paper is well-organized and presented. 

I appreciate that the performances have been greatly boosted for many datasets for dealing with label noise. 

However, as for an academic paper, I think only good empirical performance maybe not enough given that it is achieved by combining several existing methods.

content.title: Thanks for the comments.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the kind appreciation of the IEG’s strong performance.  However, we have the impression that the reviewer missed several important contributions of the paper.

First, we would like to encourage the reviewer to refer to the bundled comments above on our academic contributions, novelty and impact. 

We believe that the reviewer mistakenly thought our paper only has good empirical experience all because of combining existing things. However, it is a clear misunderstanding. We believe that the reviewer overlooked the method contributions in our paper (e.g. meta re-labeling, the key for robust training at high noise regimes, consistency to improve initial pseudo labeling, as well as detailed modification of training with strong experimental validations).

Robust training methods against noisy labels are very important in numerous deep learning applications as well as in AI research community. We believe the potential value of our technique will be important to broad audience in both industry and academia thanks to its performance leaps compared with existing methods.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary:
The paper proposed a IEG method to handle the noisy label learning problem. IEG consists of 3 parts: 1)  isolate the noise
labels via meta optimization; 2) escalate the supervision mislabeled data via pseudo meta re-labeling; 3) use small trusted data to guide training. IEG gains improvements over SOTA. 

Strength:
1. The motivation of IEG is very clear. 
2. Ablation experiments are useful for understanding. 

Weakness:
1. The organization of Section 2 is somewhat confusing. Readers may need to jump from one section to another section to follow how the method work. IEG should consist of 3 components, while there are only 2 subsections in section 2. Could the authors clarify which part corresponds to which component? 
2. I am wondering where are the tiny trusted data used? I am not following that from ALG 1. Do I miss something?
3. For experimental comparisons, I think the authors may miss some important baselines. 
    1) Symmetric cross entropy for robust learning with noisy labels, ICCV2019
    2) Joint Optimization Framework for Learning with Noisy Labels, CVPR2018
    3) Dimensionality-driven learning with noisy labels, ICML2018
4. For the ablation study, the authors miss some important experiments. 1) testing the influence of the number of trusted data; 2) showing the rate of isolated misclassified data in the learning process. 3) showing the influence of weight w. 
5. Open-set case is important for understanding IEG. I am confusing why IEG still works so well in the open-set case where most labels of data cannot be predicted correctly because of the open-set setting. The weight w before examples very small? or anything else? The author should provide more evidence on open-set case for better understanding.

display_title: Thanks for the detailed comments and questions

content.title: Thanks for the detailed comments and questions
content.comment:
Thanks for the detailed comments and finding our motivations and studies valuable.


Q1: We agree the method section is not separated by the three aspects (I,E,G). Since the three aspects are dependent, we organized it in this way for easier understanding. In general, Isolation is introduced in Section 2.1, Escalation and Guidance are introduced in Section 2.2. The three components are dependent with each other, so their introduction are a bit mixed. For example, Escalation is meta learning to re-label the mislabeled data, which requires initial pseudo labels (Section 2.2.1) and the meta step (Section 2.1).  We will improve the structure to reduce the confusing in the next version.

Q2: There are two places trusted probe data (D^p) is used. First, it is used to compute meta loss at Equation 2 (L^p), so as to obtain optimized re-weighting and re-labelling coefficients. Second, the probe data is used in Section 2.2.2, which is served as Guidance by mixup with mislabeled data. We will clarify this.

Q3: Thanks for pointing them out. We did not compare several methods in the Tables but only cite and discuss them is because our results are already significantly better than some of the strongest previous methods. So the information of making longer table is not that useful. Paper 2) is discussed and we will cite paper 1) and 3) in the next version.

Q4: Thanks for the three suggestions. Please read the following comments.

"1) testing the influence of number of trusted data": We already provide such study on CIFAR100 in Table 2. We use 0.1k, 0.5k and 1k as number of trusted data samples.

"2) Showing the rate of isolated misclassified data in the learning process" and "3) showing the influence of weight w" are referring to the same component. 

  We would like to highlight that one important contribution of this paper is meta re-labeling, which is the most critical success for handling several label noise over 80% noise ratio. We actually provide such analysis in Figure 2 (page 8). As you can see, the re-labeling coefficient (\lambda) is effective at switching between original labels for clean data and pseudo labels of mislabeled data. The performance drop without the meta re-labeling is huge (see bottom of Figure 2).

Q5: Great question! Neural nets are vulnerable to noise labels is because it can easily overfit to mislabeled data. So preventing supervision of bad data is critical. How does IEG achieve this?

    One key concept we would like to highlight is that IEG does not make any assumptions for label noise types. The method ONLY learns to learn pseudo labels and weights in a way that can optimize the performance of the trusted probe data (pls see Section 2.1) via meta learning. The only assumption here is that if the models performs well on the probe data, then they should also perform well on unseen test data.

    There are two major explanations for the success on open-set noise labels where noisy images are not from target classes. 

    1) IEG learns effective weights for each sample to avoid wrong supervision from irrelevant samples so it retains effective at open-set cases: re-weighting lowers down the weights of bad samples. The generated datasets are provided by the authors of ROG [1]. We do not have IDs of clean and noisy training images. So we can not observe oracle to compare the actual weights and pseudo labels of clean vs noisy images. Nevertheless, the image noise ratio if open-set is 60%. We observe that roughly 60% of samples in each batch get exactly zero weight, matching the ideal elimination of the amount of samples expected from the noise ratio.

    2) Our meta re-labeling replaces original labels to “pseudo-labels”. For noisy images are not irrelevant, the model will make high uncertainty predictions, so the pseudo labels will be very flat according to how we obtain the pseudo labels (see Section 2.2.1). The cross-entropy softmax loss on flat labels will not bring strong bad supervision since the losses will be closer to entropy minimization. 
It is a very useful evidence for effective methods handling real world label noises. 

[1] Lee, Kimin, et al. "Robust Inference via Generative Classifiers for Handling Noisy Labels." arXiv preprint arXiv:1901.11300 (2019).

content.title: Thanks for your suggestions.
content.comment:
Thanks for your suggestions.

This paper focuses more on general image classification and test that the method on various noise label types. The tested benchmarks are widely used in previous papers. We believe they are sufficient to validate the proposed method. 

We agree the present Food and Clothing datasets would be interesting for further validation. In our work, we used CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as they are extensively used as standard benchmarks, and we also used WebVision to validate the performance improvements on real-world tasks. We expect similar performance improvements on other datasets you mentioned, but we leave this as future work.

display_title: Learned polices do not affect the performance

content.title: Learned polices do not affect the performance
content.comment:
We agree that AutoAugment implicitly uses more labeled data than our trusted set. However, we provide the ablation studies and show that the performance gain is not due to the learned policy. Our method still keep state of the art by removing the policies, as shown in Table 7 (IEG-7). Moreover,  we test a strategy by randomizing the policies at each training batch generation instead of using the learned one, and we observe that the performance is nearly identical to the ones trained with AutoAugment.

The results suggest that the gains from learned policies are negligible. Our method remains state of the art without learned policies. 

We will update this in the next version.

content.title: Bundled responses to Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2 to justify the scientific contribution
content.comment:
We appreciate the high-level analysis and criticisms from the Reviewer 1 and 2, which helped us to clarify and improve our paper. 

To start with, we believe that the technical contributions of the paper seems are misunderstood or overlooked, potentially duo to the way the paper presented is not clear enough.
However, we think the challenge of the task we are addressing and the implications of significant performance improvements are underestimated. We would like to emphasize that in deep learning research, such leaps in performance improvement are crucial for validating research contributions.  We appreciate if the reviewers could go through the following points in our responses that underline the novelty and impact of our contributions, and consider a re-evaluation. 

Overall, our method is not a simple combination as indicated. Instead, our method is composed of novel techniques and re-designs with new discoveries of existing things in order to overcome some of the fundamental challenges. We would like to restate our academic contributions as follows:

1) Our method proposes Meta Re-labeling, a key factor for maintaining high accuracy in the high noise regimes, as opposed to other meta learning-based methods like Learning to reweight (L2R), which proposes to learn the weighting online. On the other hand, our method generalizes online learning of coefficients to online re-labeling (please see Eq. 3-5). For details of the meta-relabeling component of our method, please refer to Figure 2 (page 8). Meta re-labeling component of our method is already critical in high noise regimes, e.g. yielding over 55% accuracy with > 90% noise ratio (see Fig. 1). We would like to underline that this novel single component that has introduced for the first time with very significant performance improvements, should already warrant for sufficient academic contribution in terms of novelty. 

2) IEG is based on carefully re-designing the existing components for noise labels, sometimes with substantial changes.  For instance, to improve Escalation from mislabeled data, it is necessary to improve pseudo label quality to initialize the proposed meta re-labeling, for which we propose to generate sharper pseudo labels by encouraging consistent in prediction (as stated in Section 2.2.3). The effectiveness of this is studied in Section 3.5, showing accuracy improvements from 61% to 75% at 80% noise ratio on CIFAR100. 

    Reviewer 2 raises the concern that we combine existing Pseudo Labels and MixUp methods. However, these techniques have actually been used many times in previous methods for noise-robust learning [1,2,3] - our method is not the first attempt to combine them. However, we obtain far superior performance improvements than the alternative methods, which clearly indicates that the way we utilize the existing methods are substantially different and our design choices based on them are crucial. We encourage Reviewer 2 to thoroughly compare our method to such alternative methods to re-evaluate the importances of our design choices on how we build on the previous work.

3) Strong performance improvements given by extensive empirical studies should indicate the strength of our ideas, from a scientific perspective. Noise-robust learning has numerous real-world applications and has been a commonly-studied problem in AI community. Some of the benchmarks in noise-robust learning has been studied for many years, without very significant leaps in the achievable performance. As shown in our experiments, existing methods all suffer severely in high noise regimes (i.e. less than 50% accuracy with 80% label noises). Our method, for the first time, makes a difference and consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on various benchmarks, especially in high noise regimes (see Figure 1). 

     Our paper suggests that, in practice, there are consistent additional benefits from noisy labels (even though very noisy) than using unsupervised information. We think they are valuable contributions to the community and ML practitioners.


[1] Arazo, Eric, et al. "Unsupervised label noise modeling and loss correction." ICML 2019.
[2] Tanaka, Daiki, et al. "Joint optimization framework for learning with noisy labels." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2018.
[3] Ding, Yifan, et al. "A semi-supervised two-stage approach to learning from noisy labels." 2018 IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). IEEE, 2018.
[4] Han, Jiangfan, Ping Luo, and Xiaogang Wang. "Deep self-learning from noisy labels." Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2019.
